case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Andy Warhol’s licensing of a silkscreen portrait derived from Lynn Goldsmith’s Prince photograph was “fair use” because it was sufficiently “transformative,” especially under the first statutory fair-use factor when the use was commercial and in the same general licensing market as the original.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 17 U.S.C. § 107 (fair use) (and relatedly 17 U.S.C. § 106 exclusive rights, particularly the licensing right).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Andy Warhol Foundation argues that Warhol’s Prince Series is a paradigmatic fair use because it adds new expression, meaning, and message to Goldsmith’s photograph—transforming a realistic studio photo into a stylized pop-art commentary on celebrity and commodification. Petitioner contends the Second Circuit adopted an overly cramped and unpredictable approach to “transformative use” by discounting artistic meaning and overemphasizing market substitution, thereby threatening a wide range of follow-on artistic practices (e.g., appropriation art). Petitioner and supporting amici also stress that fair use must protect new creative works even when they are commercially exploited, and that requiring permission whenever a work is recognizably sourced would chill artistic innovation and conflict with Supreme Court guidance on transformativeness (including the Court’s more flexible, purpose-focused discussion in Google v. Oracle).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Goldsmith argues that Warhol’s work is an unauthorized derivative that appropriates the core protected expression of her photo (its depiction, composition, lighting, and pose) with insufficient justification under § 107—especially because the challenged use is commercial licensing to magazines, a market in which photographers like Goldsmith traditionally participate. Respondents maintain that “new meaning or message” cannot by itself justify copying where the secondary user competes in the same licensing market; otherwise famous artists could override photographers’ rights simply by asserting a different artistic intent. They support the Second Circuit’s insistence on an objective, work-and-use-focused inquiry (not deference to the alleged meaning of the secondary artist) and emphasize that expansive transformativeness would collapse the derivative-work right and destabilize predictable licensing markets for visual works.
key_precedents: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569 (1994)
Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc., 141 S. Ct. 1183 (2021)
Harper & Row, Publishers, Inc. v. Nation Enterprises, 471 U.S. 539 (1985)
Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc., 464 U.S. 417 (1984)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Warhol imbued the image with a different “meaning or message,” but under Campbell that cannot be dispositive when the particular use challenged is a commercial magazine license that serves the same general end as the original—illustrating a celebrity in an editorial setting—and so risks superseding the copyright holder’s ordinary licensing opportunity. Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on focusing factor one on this specific licensing transaction, rather than on the creation or gallery display of the Prince Series, is the narrowest and most administrable ground and avoids turning transformativeness into a judge-made override of § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers caution reinforces my minimalist approach: if appropriation art’s commercial relicensing warrants a broader safe harbor, Congress is better positioned to define it than an elastic “new meaning” inquiry. Harper & Row’s protection of customary markets confirms that where the secondary use competes in the licensing channel the author traditionally exploits, factor one cannot be rescued by asserted new meaning alone.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Warhol’s alterations add new aesthetics or a different “meaning or message,” but that contention cannot override § 107(1)’s textual command to evaluate the “purpose and character of the use” actually challenged—here, the Foundation’s commercial magazine-licensing transaction. As Justice Gorsuch notes, treating “new meaning” as sufficient would effectively create a judicial carveout that collapses Congress’s § 106 derivative-work and licensing rights whenever a secondary user asserts artistic intent, which is not grounded in the statute’s original public meaning. Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on market substitution in customary licensing channels aligns with Harper & Row’s teaching that fair use should not be applied to strip authors of established licensing markets central to the copyright bargain. Campbell’s transformativeness discussion, properly read, does not license courts to deem a use “different” in the abstract when the accused commercial use competes in the very market the copyright owner may exploit.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that Warhol’s work conveys a different aesthetic or “new meaning,” but Campbell does not treat that as dispositive—especially when the use is a commercial license that competes in the ordinary editorial-licensing channel. Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on evaluating the specific “use” (the Foundation’s magazine-licensing transaction) is consistent with § 107(1)’s text and avoids an atextual rule that would let asserted artistic transformation swallow § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights. Justice Kavanaugh’s practical-consequences concern also matters: if “new meaning” alone can justify commercial relicensing in adjacent markets, predictable licensing incentives for photographers collapse, which Harper & Row cautions against. No cited precedent requires us to ignore the commercial, market-substituting character of this licensing transaction, so my vote remains for respondent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that Warhol’s image conveys a new meaning or message, but Campbell does not let that consideration override the statutory focus on the specific “purpose and character of the use” actually challenged—here, a commercial magazine-licensing transaction. As Justice Kagan persuasively frames it, that licensing use overlaps directly with Goldsmith’s customary editorial-licensing market, making it functionally substitutive rather than justified by a distinct objective like parody. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow-holding approach also addresses the chilling-effects concern: we need not pass on creation or display of the Prince Series generally to conclude this particular commercial relicensing weighs against fair use, consistent with Harper & Row’s warning against undermining predictable licensing incentives. Given the real-world consequences for working photographers and other less powerful creators who depend on licensing revenue, I see no legal basis to treat “new meaning” as dispositive in this market-adjacent commercial setting.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that Warhol’s image adds new aesthetics and “meaning or message,” but Campbell ties factor one to whether the challenged use serves a distinct justificatory objective or instead supersedes the original in a relevant market, and “new meaning” cannot do all the work without destabilizing § 106’s licensing/derivative rights. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, the proper lens is the particular use challenged—commercial magazine licensing—and in that channel the Foundation’s license functions much like Goldsmith’s own editorial-license market, making it plausibly substitutive rather than purposefully different in the statutory sense. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers point reinforces the workability concern: expanding fair use here by privileging asserted artistic intent would effectively create an atextual carveout for commercial relicensing that Congress did not enact. Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on narrowing the holding to licensing (not condemning the Prince Series’ creation or gallery display) answers the chilling-effects worry while keeping the factor-one inquiry coherent and predictable.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Warhol’s image arguably conveys a different aesthetic and thus a different “meaning or message,” but that cannot be dispositive under § 107(1), which asks about the “purpose and character of the use” actually challenged here—commercial magazine licensing. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, that licensing use operates in the same functional market space Goldsmith herself licenses into, making it plausibly substitutive rather than justified by a distinct statutory “purpose” in the way parody was in Campbell. Harper & Row’s warning against fair-use expansions that usurp customary licensing markets reinforces that we should not let an elastic “new meaning” test erode Congress’s § 106 derivative-work and licensing rights. Justice Sotomayor’s narrower framing—deciding only this downstream licensing transaction, not condemning appropriation art categorically—best preserves the statutory balance without inviting a judge-made safe harbor that is difficult to square with the text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Warhol’s image adds new aesthetic meaning, but that argument proves too much because § 107(1) asks about the “purpose and character of the use” being challenged, not an abstract appraisal of artistic message. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, the relevant use here is commercial magazine licensing, and in that context the Foundation’s license occupies the same customary editorial-licensing market photographers rely on—making it functionally substitutive rather than a distinct justificatory purpose like parody in Campbell. Harper & Row reinforces that fair use cannot be expanded in a way that effectively strips authors of traditional licensing markets protected by § 106, and Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern underscores why we should not convert “new meaning” into a judge-made, open-ended exemption for commercial re-licensing. I therefore see no new legal argument that undermines my view that factor one weighs against fair use on these facts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—that Warhol’s work conveys a distinct “meaning or message”—still does not answer the statutory question in § 107(1), which asks about the “purpose and character of the use” being challenged, here a commercial magazine license. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, focusing on this specific licensing transaction keeps Campbell’s “transformative” concept tethered to whether the secondary use supersedes the original’s objects in a relevant market, and it prevents “new meaning” from becoming an atextual trump over § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights. Harper & Row, as Justice Sotomayor notes, underscores that fair use should not be expanded in a way that displaces customary licensing markets that supply the incentive to create, and the Foundation’s use operates in precisely that editorial-licensing channel. Nothing raised in conference offers a precedent-based or textual basis to treat asserted artistic transformation as dispositive where the accused use is commercial and functionally substitutive, so my vote remains for Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that Warhol’s work conveys a different meaning or message, but under Campbell that cannot be dispositive when the challenged “use” is a commercial magazine license that serves the same functional objective as the original in the editorial-licensing market. Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on the practical consequences for working photographers reinforces, in my view, that an expansive “new meaning” rule would predictably invite market substitution and erode § 106’s licensing/derivative-work rights in precisely the setting where those rights matter most. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers framing also supports a restrained, use-specific analysis: if Congress wants a broader safe harbor for commercial re-licensing of recognizable derivatives, it can create one, but we should not do so by stretching factor one beyond its statutory and precedential moorings. No colleague has identified a precedent that genuinely undermines this market-proximate, workability-focused approach, so I maintain my vote for respondent.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), Campbell v. Acuff-Rose instructs that the question is whether the challenged use “supersede[s]” the original’s purpose or instead serves a meaningfully different purpose, with commerciality weighing against fair use when the secondary use competes in the same general licensing market. Here the specific challenged act is Warhol’s commercial magazine licensing of an image derived from Goldsmith’s photo—a use closely aligned with the photographer’s traditional market—so any new “meaning or message” in the Warhol style cannot by itself justify displacement of the copyright owner’s licensing right under 17 U.S.C. § 106. Consistent with Harper & Row’s emphasis on protecting core incentives and established markets, a narrow ruling focusing on this particular licensing transaction best preserves predictable boundaries and institutional legitimacy without opining broadly on appropriation art. That approach respects precedent and avoids collapsing the derivative-work and licensing rights into an open-ended transformativeness inquiry.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 17 U.S.C. § 107 requires assessing the “purpose and character of the use,” and here the challenged use is commercial licensing of Warhol’s image to magazines—an exploitation that overlaps the ordinary licensing market protected by the copyright owner’s exclusive rights under 17 U.S.C. § 106. Under Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., the first factor’s “transformative” inquiry is contextual and does not treat any added “new meaning or message” as sufficient, especially where the secondary use is commercial and functions as a market substitute rather than a distinct purpose like parody. Consistent with Harper & Row, the commercial nature and usurpation of a traditional licensing market weigh strongly against fair use and caution against an expansive “transformative” label that would effectively collapse the derivative-work and licensing rights Congress secured. Applying the statute as written, Warhol’s licensing use is not fair use under the first factor given its commercial character and market proximity to Goldsmith’s licensing right.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), the “purpose and character” inquiry asks whether the secondary use “merely supersede[s] the objects of the original creation” or instead has a genuinely different character, and commerciality remains relevant. Campbell v. Acuff-Rose permits transformativeness to favor fair use, but it does not allow an asserted “new meaning or message” to swallow the author’s exclusive licensing and derivative-work rights under 17 U.S.C. § 106 when the accused use is commercial licensing in the same general market as the original. Here the challenged act is the Foundation’s licensing of Warhol’s image to magazines—precisely the kind of market photographers reasonably exploit—so factor one, considered in light of the practical consequences for predictable licensing markets, tilts against fair use, consistent with Harper & Row’s emphasis on protecting the value of the copyright owner’s market interests. A broader rule would risk collapsing § 106’s licensing right by permitting well-known secondary users to repackage the original for the same commercial purpose while claiming transformation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), the first factor asks whether the challenged “use” has a sufficiently different purpose and character, but here the specific use is commercial magazine-licensing of an image of Prince—a purpose that directly overlaps with Goldsmith’s ordinary licensing market as a photographer. Campbell v. Acuff-Rose makes clear that “transformative” meaning or message does not end the inquiry and that commercial use, especially where it risks serving as a substitute, weighs against fair use and ties closely to the fourth factor’s focus on market usurpation. Treating Warhol’s licensing as fair use on the basis of asserted new meaning would effectively collapse the § 106 derivative-work and licensing rights for working photographers, with the heaviest practical burden falling on less powerful creators who rely on predictable licensing income. Because the licensing use competes in the same general market and threatens to displace the original’s licensing value, factors one and four together favor Goldsmith.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), the “purpose and character” inquiry asks whether the challenged use has a different objective that does not “supersede” the original, and commercial exploitation weighs against fair use when the secondary use serves the same general function in the same licensing market. Here the specific challenged conduct is Warhol’s magazine-licensing of the Prince image—precisely the kind of market photographers like Goldsmith license into—so the use looks less like a transformative repurposing and more like a substitute for the original’s licensing value, implicating § 106’s exclusive rights (including the derivative-work and licensing interests). Campbell v. Acuff-Rose permits commercial transformative uses (like parody), but it ties transformativeness to a distinct justificatory purpose and cautions that factor one cannot be read to swallow the author’s § 106 rights when the secondary use competes in the same market. Consistent with Harper & Row’s emphasis on protecting core licensing markets, factor one here cuts against fair use despite any new “meaning or message,” because the use is commercial and not sufficiently different in function to justify copying in this context.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 107 directs courts to assess the “purpose and character of the use,” and Warhol’s challenged use was commercial licensing of an image of Prince to a magazine—functionally the same sort of use Goldsmith herself licenses under her exclusive rights in § 106. Under Campbell v. Acuff-Rose, “transformative” use asks whether the new work “supersede[s]” the original’s objects or instead serves a distinct purpose; where the secondary user enters the same licensing market, a claimed “new meaning or message” cannot alone erase the statutory line between fair use and the derivative-works right. Harper & Row underscores that market substitution is central in fair use analysis, and allowing a different aesthetic presentation to justify competing commercial licensing would risk collapsing § 106’s licensing and derivative-work protections into an open-ended judicial exception. Applying the statute’s text and separation-of-powers principles, any broader exemption for commercial licensing of recognizable derivatives is for Congress, not courts, to supply.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), the first factor focuses on the “purpose and character” of the challenged use, including whether it is transformative, but Campbell v. Acuff-Rose also instructs that commerciality still “tends to weigh against” fair use and that the inquiry asks whether the secondary use “supersede[s] the objects” of the original. Here, the specific challenged act is Warhol’s commercial licensing of an image derived from Goldsmith’s photograph to magazines—a use that targets the same general licensing market protected by § 106 and traditionally served by photographers—so the transformativeness asserted at the level of artistic meaning does not justify market-substituting commercial exploitation. Consistent with Harper & Row’s emphasis on protecting the author’s right to exploit customary markets and with an institutionalist concern for predictable, workable rules, an expansive “new meaning or message” test in this licensing context would erode the derivative-work/licensing rights Congress secured and destabilize settled expectations. Given the commercial, non-commentary licensing use and its proximity to the original’s market, the first factor (and practical workability) favors Goldsmith.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 107(1) directs courts to assess the “purpose and character of the use,” including whether it is commercial; here, the challenged act is Warhol Foundation’s commercial licensing of an image of Prince to magazines—a use that shares the same general licensing purpose as Goldsmith’s photograph and thus weighs against fair use. Under Campbell v. Acuff-Rose, “transformative” use turns on whether the secondary use adds a further purpose or different character rather than merely superseding the original, but “new meaning or message” cannot do all the work where the secondary use competes in a traditional licensing market protected by § 106. Consistent with Harper & Row’s emphasis on protecting the copyright owner’s licensing interests and with Campbell’s concern that fair use not swallow the derivative-work right, the first factor favors Goldsmith because the Foundation’s use is commercial and functionally substitutive in the relevant market for magazine illustration licenses. Precedent and methodological consistency therefore counsel rejecting a transformativeness theory that would allow commercial re-licensing of a copyrighted photograph based chiefly on asserted artistic meaning.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), Campbell v. Acuff-Rose directs courts to ask whether the secondary use "supersede[s] the objects" of the original or instead has a meaningfully different purpose, while also accounting for commerciality; here, the challenged act is Warhol’s commercial licensing of the image to magazines, a use that overlaps with the ordinary editorial-licensing purpose of Goldsmith’s photograph. Even if the Prince Series reflects a different artistic "meaning or message," that alone cannot carry the first factor when the use is functionally a substitute in the same general licensing market, because that would erode the § 106 derivative-work and licensing rights. Consistent with Harper & Row and Campbell’s instruction to consider the factors in light of copyright’s aims, factor four’s market-harm concern reinforces that this particular licensing use is not fair where it competes with photographers’ traditional licensing revenue streams. On this record, procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel against a rule that allows a famous secondary artist to displace the original creator’s licensing opportunity simply by asserting transformativeness.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Andy Warhol’s licensing of a silkscreen portrait derived from Lynn Goldsmith’s photograph for magazine publication qualifies as “fair use,” particularly under the first factor’s “purpose and character” inquiry (including transformativeness).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 17 U.S.C. § 107 (fair use) (and relatedly 17 U.S.C. § 106 exclusive rights, especially the right to prepare derivative works and to license reproductions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Andy Warhol Foundation argues that Warhol’s Prince Series works are quintessentially transformative because they imbue Goldsmith’s photo with a materially different meaning/message and aesthetic (Warhol’s pop-art commentary on celebrity and mass media), so factor one should strongly favor fair use without requiring that the secondary work comment on the original itself. It further contends that treating such works as infringing derivative works would chill core artistic practices (appropriation, collage, recontextualization) and conflict with Supreme Court fair-use principles as applied to transformative uses. The Foundation also downplays market harm by emphasizing that licensing an Andy Warhol image is not a market substitute for licensing a realistic celebrity photograph, and that Goldsmith’s claimed market is defined too broadly if it captures all later works that depict Prince.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Goldsmith argues Warhol copied protectable expressive elements of her photograph and produced works that, at least as used here (commercial licensing to magazines), serve substantially the same purpose as her photo—illustrating stories about Prince—thereby usurping her licensing market. She contends that “transformativeness” cannot be satisfied merely by asserting a new meaning or style when the secondary use supersedes the original’s function in the same commercial market, and that granting fair use here would effectively create a broad “famous-artist exception” that undermines photographers’ derivative-work and licensing rights. On factor four, she stresses that Condé Nast’s paid license for Warhol’s image is direct evidence of market substitution in the relevant editorial-illustration licensing market.
key_precedents: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569 (1994)
Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc., 141 S. Ct. 1183 (2021)
Harper & Row, Publishers, Inc. v. Nation Enterprises, 471 U.S. 539 (1985)
Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc., 464 U.S. 417 (1984)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that Warhol’s alterations add a different meaning or message and thus are “transformative” under Campbell, but that cannot be evaluated in the abstract without unmooring § 107(1) from the challenged “use.” As Justice Kagan persuasively stresses, the use at issue is the Foundation’s commercial license to a magazine to illustrate a story about Prince, a purpose that substantially overlaps Goldsmith’s own editorial-illustration licensing market and therefore tends to “supersede the objects” of the original in Campbell’s terms. Justice Thomas’s statutory-structure point reinforces my concern that a free-floating “new message” test would erode § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights, and Harper & Row’s caution against reallocating value from established licensing markets supports a narrow, market-substitution-focused holding. A minimal, fact-bound ruling against fair use for this specific magazine-licensing transaction best preserves precedent and institutional legitimacy without sweeping judgments about museum display or other contexts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest contention remains that Warhol’s work conveys a new “meaning or message,” but that is not the test § 107(1) supplies; the text asks about the “purpose and character of the use,” and here the use is a commercial magazine license that operates in the same editorial-illustration channel Goldsmith exploits. Chief Justice Roberts’s point is decisive under a textualist reading: anchoring factor one to the specific licensing transaction keeps Campbell’s transformativeness concept from becoming a free-floating, subjective aesthetic inquiry that effectively overrides § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights. Harper & Row further reinforces that when the challenged use is commercial and market-substituting in a traditional licensing market, fair use should not be expanded to reallocate that market from the copyright owner to the copier. Justice Gorsuch’s statutory-coherence concern also confirms that adopting petitioner’s “new message” approach would invite courts to craft an extra-textual exception untethered to the statute’s structure.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point is that Warhol’s image conveys a different aesthetic and “meaning,” but § 107(1) asks about the purpose and character of the challenged use, and here that use is the Foundation’s commercial license to a magazine to illustrate a story about Prince—functionally the same editorial-illustration purpose Goldsmith’s photo serves. As Justice Roberts emphasizes, focusing on the particular licensing transaction keeps Campbell’s “transformative” concept tethered to whether the secondary use supersedes the original’s market function rather than to subjective artistic claims. Harper & Row’s warning against commercial appropriation that displaces a copyright owner’s traditional licensing markets, together with § 106’s protection for derivative and licensing rights, makes it impractical and textually unsound to treat this market-substituting license as fair use. I therefore remain with the respondent: factor one (and correspondingly factor four) weigh against fair use on these facts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that Warhol’s stylistic changes supply a new meaning or message and thus are transformative under Campbell, but that approach becomes untethered from § 107(1)’s command to evaluate the specific “use” at issue. As Justice Kagan persuasively stresses, the challenged conduct here is a paid magazine license to illustrate a Prince story—an editorial-illustration purpose that materially overlaps Goldsmith’s own licensing market and therefore looks substitutive rather than “further” in the Campbell sense. Justice Gorsuch’s statutory-coherence point reinforces that adopting a broad, subjective “new message” test would erode § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights and invite a status-tilted regime in which well-known artists can commercially appropriate photographs in the very markets photographers depend on. Harper & Row’s warning about protecting core commercial exploitation and the record evidence that Condé Nast paid AWF instead of Goldsmith keep factors one and four aligned against fair use on these facts, so I do not see a legal argument that undermines my position.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best argument remains that Warhol added a distinct meaning or message, but under § 107(1) that cannot be evaluated in the abstract; it must be tied to the particular “purpose and character” of the challenged use—AWF’s commercial license to a magazine to illustrate a Prince story. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Campbell’s “supersede the objects” framing keeps factor one anchored to whether the secondary use functions as a market-facing substitute, and this licensing transaction overlaps Goldsmith’s ordinary editorial-illustration market rather than serving a different purpose like criticism or commentary. Justice Gorsuch’s statutory-coherence point reinforces that a freestanding “new meaning” test would unpredictably erode § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights by turning artistic assertion into a broad exception. Harper & Row, cited by several colleagues including Justice Sotomayor, further supports treating commercial exploitation in a traditional licensing channel as weighing against fair use even if the secondary work differs aesthetically.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Petitioner’s best point remains Campbell’s language about “new meaning or message,” but that cannot become a free-floating aesthetic test divorced from what § 107(1) directs us to examine: the purpose and character of the challenged use. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, the use at issue is AWF’s commercial magazine license to illustrate a story about Prince—a purpose that materially overlaps Goldsmith’s own editorial-licensing market and therefore looks like a substitute rather than a further, distinct end. Justice Thomas’s separation-of-powers/textual concern reinforces my view that expanding “transformativeness” to swallow § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights would be a judicial rewrite of the statutory scheme, something Harper & Row warns against in market-displacement settings. Nothing raised in conference undermines that statutory, market-anchored analysis, so I remain with the Respondent on these facts.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains that Warhol’s alterations add new meaning and thus are “transformative” under Campbell, but that framing risks turning factor one into an untethered aesthetic inquiry that eclipses the statute’s focus on the challenged use. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 107(1) directs us to assess the purpose and character of AWF’s specific use here—a commercial magazine license for Prince editorial illustration—which substantially overlaps Goldsmith’s own licensing purpose and looks substitutive rather than distinct. Justice Thomas’s statutory-structure concern reinforces that an abstract “new meaning” test would effectively erode § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights by judicial gloss, contrary to Harper & Row’s caution about commercial market substitution. A narrow ruling limited to this licensing context preserves space for criticism or commentary uses while maintaining settled expectations in photo-licensing markets.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Petitioner’s strongest point remains that Warhol’s alterations inject a new “meaning or message,” but Campbell’s transformativeness inquiry cannot be untethered from § 107(1)’s focus on the particular “purpose and character” of the challenged use. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the use here is AWF’s commercial licensing to a magazine to illustrate a story about Prince—substantially overlapping Goldsmith’s own editorial-illustration licensing purpose—so it looks like market-facing substitution rather than a different end. Justice Thomas’s statutory-structure concern reinforces that a broad “new meaning” test would improperly erode § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights by converting aesthetic recharacterization into a near-categorical defense. Harper & Row’s warning about reallocating value from the copyright owner in traditional licensing markets therefore continues to support weighting factor one (and, correspondingly, factor four) against fair use on these facts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that Warhol’s alterations communicate a different meaning or message, but Campbell does not license an untethered aesthetic inquiry; it directs us to ask whether the challenged use "supersede[s] the objects" of the original in context. As Justice Sotomayor and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, the use before us is AWF’s commercial magazine licensing to illustrate a Prince story—functionally overlapping Goldsmith’s ordinary editorial-illustration licensing purpose—so factor one weighs against fair use. Harper & Row’s focus on practical market consequences strengthens that conclusion, especially given the concrete evidence that Condé Nast paid AWF rather than Goldsmith, reflecting market substitution rather than a distinct purpose. I also share Justice Thomas’s concern that treating “new message” as dispositive would erode § 106’s licensing and derivative-work rights in a way that predictably disadvantages less powerful creators who rely on those markets.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107 factor one, the relevant “purpose and character” inquiry turns on the use at issue—here, the Foundation’s commercial licensing of Warhol’s image to a magazine to illustrate a story about Prince—an objective purpose that substantially overlaps with Goldsmith’s own editorial-illustration licensing market. Campbell v. Acuff-Rose instructs that transformativeness requires that the secondary use not “merely supersede the objects of the original creation,” and the commercial nature of a use remains relevant where, as here, the secondary use competes in the same licensing channel. Harper & Row reinforces that fair use should not be used to appropriate the “heart” of protected expression in a way that displaces the copyright holder’s traditional markets, a concern echoed by factor four’s focus on “the potential market” for licensing and derivative uses protected by § 106. A narrow holding rejecting fair use on these specific licensing facts best respects precedent and preserves copyright’s market structure without announcing any broad rule about museum display or noncommercial fine-art creation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 107(1) directs courts to consider the “purpose and character” of the use, including its commercial nature, and nothing in the statute elevates a freewheeling “new meaning or message” test that would swallow § 106’s exclusive rights—especially the right to prepare and license derivative works. Here the challenged use is Warhol’s commercial licensing of a portrait to a magazine to illustrate stories about Prince, a purpose that closely tracks the ordinary editorial-illustration purpose for which Goldsmith licenses photographs, weighing against fair use under factor one and confirming market substitution concerns under § 107(4). As Harper & Row emphasized, fair use is a limited exception that should not be construed to negate the author’s core statutory rights, and Campbell’s discussion of “transformative” use cannot be read to authorize broad appropriation whenever an artist claims a different message. Because extending “transformative use” this far would effectively displace the derivative-work right codified in §§ 101 and 106, I would hold the licensing use not fair.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. §§ 106 and 107, the Foundation’s challenged use is Warhol’s commercial licensing of the image to illustrate a magazine story about Prince—a purpose closely aligned with the photograph’s own licensing function—so factor one disfavors fair use notwithstanding any claimed new “meaning” or style. As Harper & Row emphasizes, commercial exploitation that supplants the copyright holder’s right to license first publication or derivative uses weighs strongly against fair use, and the fourth factor—market harm—remains central where the secondary use usurps a traditional, reasonably foreseeable licensing market. Campbell permits consideration of “transformativeness,” but it also warns that copying the “heart” of the work and serving as a market substitute supports a finding of unfair use, especially when the accused use competes in the same editorial-illustration market. Treating Warhol’s commercial magazine license as fair use would dilute the statutory derivative-work and licensing rights in § 106 and create an impractical rule turning on subjective assertions of new message rather than the concrete market consequences the statute is designed to protect.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), Campbell instructs courts to ask whether the secondary use “supersede[s] the objects of the original creation” or instead adds a different purpose and character, and commerciality remains relevant where the later use competes in the same licensing market. Here, the challenged use is Warhol’s commercial licensing of the image to illustrate a magazine story about Prince—substantially the same objective served by licensing Goldsmith’s photograph—so the “purpose and character” inquiry weighs against fair use notwithstanding Warhol’s stylistic alterations or asserted new meaning. That conclusion aligns with Harper & Row’s emphasis on protecting the author’s right to control first-order commercial exploitation and with § 106’s grant of exclusive rights to license reproductions and derivative uses in that market. Factor four reinforces this: Condé Nast’s paid license for Warhol’s image is concrete evidence of market substitution in the editorial-illustration licensing sphere, and fair use should not become a de facto exception that strips working photographers of practical access to remedies and fair compensation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), the relevant “purpose and character” inquiry focuses on the challenged use—here, the Foundation’s commercial licensing of Warhol’s image to a magazine to illustrate a story about Prince—which closely tracks the ordinary purpose of Goldsmith’s photograph in the same editorial-illustration market. Campbell v. Acuff-Rose makes clear that transformativeness turns on whether the secondary use “supersede[s] the objects of the original creation,” and commerciality, while not dispositive, matters when the use is a market-facing substitute rather than commentary or a distinct purpose. Giving dispositive weight to a claimed new “meaning or message” divorced from the actual licensing use would risk collapsing § 106’s derivative-work and reproduction rights into a broad “style/meaning” exception, undermining statutory coherence and workability. Consistent with Harper & Row, the first factor here—considered with the commercial licensing context and its market-substituting character—favors Goldsmith rather than fair use.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 107’s first factor asks about the “purpose and character” of the challenged use, and here the specific use is AWF’s commercial licensing of Warhol’s image to a magazine to illustrate a story about Prince—functionally the same kind of editorial-illustration purpose Goldsmith licenses photographs for, which indicates the secondary use “supersede[s] the objects of the original” rather than serving a distinct purpose. Campbell v. Acuff-Rose instructs that “transformative” use turns on whether the new work adds new expression, meaning, or message, but it does not authorize a broad carveout that would collapse § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights whenever a secondary user can articulate a new aesthetic; when the secondary use competes in the same commercial licensing market, the commercial character weighs against fair use under § 107(1). Harper & Row reinforces that fair use cannot be used to appropriate the copyright owner’s right to exploit the work’s market, and factor one must be read in harmony with § 106 rather than as a license to redistribute commercial value to the copier. Given separation-of-powers concerns, courts should not enlarge fair use beyond the statutory text in a way that effectively rewrites the derivative-works boundary Congress established.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), the relevant inquiry focuses on the specific use at issue—commercial licensing of Warhol’s image to a magazine to illustrate a story about Prince—which largely shares the same purpose as Goldsmith’s photograph (editorial illustration), weighing against fair use despite any asserted new artistic meaning. Campbell v. Acuff-Rose recognizes that “transformativeness” turns on whether the secondary use adds something new rather than superseding the original, and here the challenged licensing use functions as a substitute in the same market, implicating Goldsmith’s § 106 rights to reproduce and license derivative uses. Consistent with Harper & Row, the commercial nature and the displacement of the copyright holder’s traditional licensing market are powerful considerations that counsel restraint in expanding fair use. A rule allowing a new “meaning or message” to justify commercial substitution would be difficult to administer and would risk undermining settled expectations in established photo-licensing markets.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the text of 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), the "purpose and character" inquiry asks whether the challenged use "supersede[s] the objects" of the original, not merely whether it can be described as having a different meaning or aesthetic. Campbell instructs that transformativeness is tied to whether the secondary use serves a further purpose or different character, and it also cautions that commercial exploitation remains relevant and that a claimed new purpose does not confer a free pass. Here, Warhol’s licensing of the image to illustrate a magazine story about Prince is a paradigmatic commercial, substitutive use in the same editorial-illustration licensing market as Goldsmith’s photograph, implicating both § 106’s derivative-work and licensing rights and factor four’s market-substitution concern recognized in Harper & Row. Consistent with methodological restraint, extending “transformative” to cover this kind of competing commercial license would risk collapsing § 106’s derivative-work right and turning fair use into a broad, style-based exemption untethered to the statute’s text and Campbell’s focus on substitutive purpose.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under 17 U.S.C. § 107(1), the relevant “purpose and character” is Warhol’s commercial licensing of the image to a magazine to illustrate a story about Prince—an end that substantially overlaps with the ordinary editorial-illustration purpose for which Goldsmith licenses photographs, and thus tends to “supersede the objects of the original creation” rather than meaningfully change the use in context. Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music instructs that transformativeness is not a free-standing “new meaning” inquiry; it is assessed alongside commerciality and in relation to whether the secondary use serves a different purpose, and here the commercial licensing use cuts strongly against fair use. Consistent with Harper & Row, the first factor cannot be divorced from practical market consequences, and the record of Condé Nast paying for the Warhol license supports the conclusion that the challenged use intrudes on Goldsmith’s protected licensing market under § 106, reinforcing that this is not fair use. Procedural fairness and equal protection concerns counsel against a rule that would effectively privilege famous artists’ stylistic reworkings while eroding photographers’ ability to control and license derivative and reproductions in the same commercial market.
